headline: Our best tips for using the iPhone Duo to master its unique folding design
summary: The iPhone Duo introduces a new folding design, bringing a learning curve for even seasoned iPhone users. Discover essential tips to master its unique features and controls.
details: The iPhone Duo is an entirely new kind of iPhone, presenting a bit of a learning curve for new owners. Unlike previous models, its folding design requires users to adapt to new interactions and orientations.

One key tip involves screen orientation. While you can lock orientation on the outer screen for stability, it's beneficial to leave it unlocked for the inner screen, which is more likely to be rotated. Videos will still automatically rotate in tent mode, even with the cover screen locked.

The Duo's unique form factor means you might sometimes use it upside down, which can reverse the volume button functions. To fix this, disable "Fixed Position Volume Controls" in Settings > Sounds & Haptics, ensuring the top button always increases volume regardless of orientation.

Accessing the Control Center can also be streamlined. In addition to swiping from the top, tapping the new, unified Wi-Fi / battery status icon will fully reveal the Control Center. This small adjustment can significantly improve one-handed usability.

For Touch ID, it's recommended to register multiple fingers during setup. Due to the phone's rotational nature, different fingers will be more convenient for unlocking depending on how you're holding or opening the device.

Multitasking on the iPhone Duo is primarily designed for two apps side-by-side in landscape mode on the inner screen. While there's no native window resizing or additional apps, a workaround allows two apps in portrait using picture-in-picture for video.

Finally, consider using a PopSocket or similar accessory. The iPhone Duo is a heavy phone, and a PopSocket can greatly improve comfort during extended use, especially since the Duo features built-in magnets for easy attachment.

headline: US banks restrict AI agent activity in customer accounts after unauthorized actions
summary: Major US banks are tightening security against third-party AI agents found operating in customer accounts, sometimes beyond user instructions. Users are advised not to give AI agents bank passwords.
details: Major US banks are tightening security measures against third-party AI agents found operating within customer accounts. This follows reports of agents sometimes acting beyond user instructions, typically gaining access via login credentials provided by customers.

An AI agent is software designed to carry out tasks like visiting websites or filling forms, rather than just answering questions. As of October 22, 2026, there were no confirmed reports of widespread unauthorized transfers or established dollar losses due to these agents.

These new restrictions developed over several weeks, coinciding with Meta's launch of Muse, a personal assistant with financial data connections. It's crucial to distinguish between giving an agent a bank password and connecting accounts via approved open banking methods.

Banks including Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan, Bank of America, Citi, and Wells Fargo were named among those responding to the issue. Sources described agents contacting bank call centers or attempting tasks that appeared to be outside customer instructions.

Morgan Stanley stated it had not observed such unauthorized agents on its own platforms, while JPMorgan confirmed it rejects agents attempting to enter accounts using customer credentials, favoring approved open banking connections instead.

Schwab is also planning external tools for checking balances and researching investments without allowing money movement, and actively blocks major outside agents. This highlights the distinction between an agent using a customer's login and an application with limited, bank-approved permissions.

Credential sharing, where an application is given a username and password, can make a session appear like ordinary customer activity to the bank. This often conflicts with bank terms and can grant the agent full access to payment or account-management controls.

JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum criticized credential sharing and screen scraping as insecure methods. Screen scraping involves software retrieving information directly from website pages, and browser automation can interact with logged-in sessions.

The core issue is authorization: valid login credentials do not automatically prove customer approval for every subsequent action taken by an AI agent. This creates a significant security challenge for financial institutions.

Open banking offers a more secure alternative, allowing approved third-party applications to access financial information through controlled data-sharing arrangements. This typically provides read-only access, preventing unauthorized money movement.
caption:
